passages.original: quod se consequi posse diffident. Verum tamen, quod in Oratore iam M. Tullius rectissime dixit, par est eos, qui generi humano res utilissimas conquirere et perpensas exploratasque memoriae tradere concupierint, cuncta temptare.Nec si vel illa praestantis ingenii vis vel inclitarum artium defecerit instrumentum, confestim debemus ad otium et inertiam devolvi, sed quod sapienter speraverimus,perseveranter consectari.
passages.english: what they despair of being able to attain. But nevertheless, as Marcus Tullius has already said most rightly in the Orator, it is fitting that those who have longed to search out things most useful to the human race, and to hand them down to memory once weighed and tested, should attempt everything. Nor, if either that force of outstanding talent or the equipment of the renowned arts should fail us, ought we at once to sink into idleness and inertia; rather we should pursue with perseverance what we have wisely hoped for.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the subject of 'they despair' lies in the preceding text. 'Orator' refers to Cicero's work of that name.

passages.original: Nam in rusticatione vel antiquissima est ratio pascendi eademque quaestuosissima, propter quod nomina quoque pecuniae et peculii tracta videntur a pecore: quoniam et solum id veteres possederunt, et adhuc apud quasdam gentes unum hoc usurpatur divitiarum genus: sed ne apud nostros quidem colonos alia res uberior.Ut etiam M. Cato prodidit,qui consulenti, quam partem rei rusticae exercendo celeriter locupletari posset respondit: Si bene is pasceret;rursusque interrogant, quid deinde faciendo satis uberes fructus percepturus esset, affirmavit: Si mediocriter pasceret.
passages.english: For in husbandry the system of pasturing [livestock] is both the most ancient and the most profitable, on which account even the words pecunia (money) and peculium (private property) seem to have been drawn from pecus (livestock): since the ancients possessed this alone, and among certain peoples this is still the only kind of wealth in use; and not even among our own farmers is anything else more productive. As Marcus Cato also recorded, who, when someone consulted him as to what branch of farming he might practise to grow rich quickly, replied: 'If he pastured well'; and when he was asked again what he should do next to reap sufficiently rich returns, he declared: 'If he pastured moderately well.'
passages.notes: 'interrogant' in the text is presumably for 'interrogatus' or 'interroganti'; translated in that sense.

passages.original: nostri laboris est particeps. Nec dubium, quin, ut ait Varro, ceteras pecudes bos honore superare debeat, praesertim in Italia, quae ab hoc nuncupationem. traxisse creditur, quod olim Graeci tauros italos vocabant,et in ea urbe, cuius moenibus condendis mas et femina boves aratro terminum signaverunt, vel, ut antiquiora repetam,quod item Atticis Athenis Cereris et Triptolemi fertur minister: quod inter fulgentissima sidera particeps caeli sit: quod deinde laboriosissimus adhuc hominis socius in agricultura: cuius tanta fuit apud antiquos veneratio, ut tam capitale esset bovem necuisse, quam civem.
passages.english: [the ox] shares in our labour. Nor is there any doubt that, as Varro says, the ox ought to surpass the other livestock in honour, especially in Italy, which is believed to have taken its name from it, because the Greeks of old called bulls *italoi*; and in that city at the founding of whose walls a male and a female ox marked out the boundary with the plough; or, to go back to more ancient things, because the ox is likewise said to have been the servant of Ceres and Triptolemus at Athens in Attica; because it has a share in the sky among the most brilliant stars; because, further, it is still the most hard-working companion of man in agriculture; and such was the veneration for it among the ancients that it was as much a capital offence to have killed an ox as a citizen.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the subject (the ox) is supplied from the sense. 'nuncupationem.' has a stray full stop, read as continuous. 'necuisse' is taken as 'necavisse/necuisse' (to have killed). The clause 'et in ea urbe...' is grammatically loose (likely an implied 'especially' or 'honoured'), translated as parallel to 'in Italia'. The constellation alluded to is presumably Taurus.
